To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the relevance of an entity in an event should be derived from the event it is associated with; (2) the relevance of a document with respect to the topic should be derived from other documents that discuss the topic, not from a knowledge base that is not topic-specific.

the relevance of named entities in an event is derived from the relevance of the event terms they relate to; the semantic relevance of an event is derived using a topic-specific knowledge base; and the PageRank ranking algorithm can be used to estimate the significance for an event to be included in an event-based summary.

(1) event-based summarization is more effective than topic-based summarization; (2) the relevance derived from the internal association, semantic similarity and distributional similarity of event terms is more effective than the relevance derived from a general knowledge base like WordNet; (3) the relevance derived using the internal association of event terms and the named entities associated is more effective than relevance derived using the named entities only.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extraction of event terms, and their relevance for summarization, and the results show that the relevance of event terms and named entities is a promising approach for event-based summarization.
the following questions: (1) How can we identify the event terms in documents?
the problem of how to use the event terms to derive the event relevance, and how to use the derived relevance for event-based summarization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method is effective in extracting event-based summaries.
the relevance derived from the event itself is the most effective, followed by the relevance from the document itself, and the least effective is the relevance from the knowledge base.

the event relevance derived using the internal association and semantic relatedness of the event terms and the distributional similarity of the named entities associated with the terms, along with their clustering in documents, can be used effectively in event-based summarization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the relevance of named entities is more important than the event terms themselves in the event-based summarization, and the relevance of named entity is more important than that of the event term itself in the event-based summary.

our event-based extractive summarization system outperforms the state-of-the-art systems in the DUC 1998 and 2001 test sets, and achieves the best performance among the systems that are submitted in DUC 2003.

the event relevance derived from both the intra- and inter-relevant information can significantly improve the event-based summarization performance, and the named entities associated with the event terms are the best source of information for the relevance derivation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the relevance of an event for summary can be derived from its internal association and semantic relatedness with other events, and the significance of an entity in an event is determined by the significance of the event.
the relevance of an event for summarization is better measured by considering both the event terms and the named entities associated with the event.

the event-based summarization can be improved by exploiting the information of the internal and external association between events, the semantic relatedness of event terms, and the distributional similarity of event terms.
